method: 3 subagents read the local primary PDFs vs the extracted-limits JSON; Tier-1 toxics + Sn; infant/child matrices

discrepancies.evidence: 3.2.17.1 'powder ... manufactured from cows' milk proteins or cow's milk protein hydrolysates' = 0,010; 3.2.17.3 'powder ... manufactured from soy protein isolates' = 0,020
discrepancies.note: EU splits this cell by protein source, which the JSON does not capture. Cow's-milk-based formula powder (the majority of the market) = 0.010 mg/kg, HALF the JSON's stated 0.02. The JSON's 0.02 matches only the soy-protein-isolate sub-case (3.2.17.3). Presenting 0.02 as a single undifferentiated value overstates the permitted Cd level for ordinary dairy-based formula by 2x. JSON also cites 'Section 3.2.1' which is wrong (3.2.1 is fruits/tree nuts); real section is 3.2.17.

discrepancies.evidence: 3.2.17.2 'liquid ... cows' milk proteins' = 0,005; 3.2.17.4 'liquid ... soy protein isolates' = 0,010
discrepancies.note: Same cow's-milk/soy split as the powder row. Cow's-milk-based liquid formula = 0.005 mg/kg, HALF the JSON's stated 0.01. JSON's 0.01 matches only the soy sub-case (3.2.17.4). JSON cites 'Section 3.2.1' (wrong); real section is 3.2.17.

discrepancies.food_category: Dietary foods for special medical purposes for infants and young children (powder)
discrepancies.evidence: 3.2.17.1 (FSMP is folded into the SAME combined heading 3.2.17 as infant/follow-on formula) cow's-milk powder = 0,010; soy powder (3.2.17.3) = 0,020
discrepancies.note: EU does not give FSMP its own Cd section distinct from infant formula -- 3.2.17's heading explicitly reads 'Infant formulae, follow-on formulae, food for special medical purposes intended for infants and young children ... and young-child formulae' as ONE combined line item, split only by protein source and physical form, not by formula-vs-FSMP. The JSON's separate 'Section 3.2.3' citation does not exist for Cd; there is no distinct FSMP subsection. Cow's-milk basis = 0.010 (half the JSON's 0.02); JSON value matches only the soy sub-case.

discrepancies.food_category: Dietary foods for special medical purposes for infants and young children (liquid)
discrepancies.evidence: 3.2.17.2 cow's-milk liquid = 0,005; soy liquid (3.2.17.4) = 0,010
discrepancies.note: Same combined-heading issue as the powder row. Cow's-milk basis = 0.005 (half the JSON's 0.01). No standalone 'Section 3.2.3' exists in the primary text.

discrepancies.evidence: Section 3.3 Mercury contains only 3.3.1 (fishery products/bivalve molluscs), 3.3.2 (food supplements = 0,10) and 3.3.3 (salt = 0,10). No infant-formula or follow-on-formula line item exists.
discrepancies.note: No EU mercury maximum level exists for infant/follow-on formula in Reg. (EU) 2023/915. This JSON row appears to be fabricated or mis-transcribed from another substance's infant-formula entry (e.g. the PAH or melamine recitals, which do discuss infant-formula-specific physical-form splits, at similar 0,01-scale magnitude). The cited 'EU_Regulation_2024-1756_Amendment.pdf' in raw/ is also not primary law -- it is a third-party COLEAD/AGRINFO newsletter summarizing a wording-clarification corrigendum (PAH powder/liquid split, ochratoxin wording, etc.); it does not add or amend any mercury limit.

discrepancies.food_category: Processed cereal-based foods and baby foods for infants and young children
discrepancies.evidence: Section 3.3 Mercury: only fishery products/bivalves (3.3.1), food supplements (3.3.2 = 0,10), salt (3.3.3 = 0,10). No baby-food/cereal line item.
discrepancies.note: Same as above -- no EU mercury ML exists for baby food or processed cereal-based food for infants/young children in Reg. (EU) 2023/915 or in the 2024/1756 corrigendum summary reviewed.

discrepancies.food_category: Processed cereal-based foods for infants and young children (rice-based)
discrepancies.evidence: 3.4.3 'Baby food' = 0,020 (applies to the finished product 'as placed on the market', no rice-based carve-out). The 0,10 figure the JSON cites is actually 3.4.1.5 'Rice destined for the production of food for infants and young children' -- a raw-INGREDIENT specification, not a finished-product category.
discrepancies.note: Category conflation. EU Annex I has no separate, looser finished-product iAs limit for 'rice-based' baby food/cereal -- ALL baby food and processed cereal-based food for infants/young children, rice-based or not, is capped at 0,020 mg/kg under 3.4.3. The 0,10 mg/kg value the JSON attaches to this row is the raw-material limit for rice AS AN INGREDIENT destined for infant-food manufacture (3.4.1.5), which is a different regulatory object entirely. As written, the JSON implies a finished rice cereal product may legally contain 5x more inorganic arsenic than EU law actually permits.

discrepancies.food_category: Infant formulae and follow-on formulae (rice-based, powder)
discrepancies.evidence: 3.4.2 'Infant formulae, follow-on formulae and food for special medical purposes ... and young-child formulae' has NO rice-based split; 3.4.2.1 (powder, any composition) = 0,020.
discrepancies.note: No rice-based carve-out exists for infant/follow-on formula arsenic limits under EU law -- the 0,020 mg/kg powder limit (3.4.2.1) applies uniformly regardless of rice content. This JSON row's category and value do not correspond to anything in the primary text; the real, only applicable powder-formula limit is 5x lower (0.020, not 0.1).

discrepancies.food_category: Canned infant formulae and follow-on formulae
discrepancies.evidence: 3.5.3 'Canned infant formulae, canned follow-on formulae and canned young-child formulae' = 50. Remark: 'Except canned dried and canned powdered products. The maximum level applies to the product as placed on the market.'
discrepancies.note: Value/unit correct, but the primary text explicitly EXCLUDES canned dried/canned powdered formula from this 50 mg/kg cap -- it applies to canned wet/liquid product only. The JSON's food_category ('Canned infant formulae and follow-on formulae') does not carry this exclusion and could be misread as covering canned powder tins too. Also: JSON cites 'Section 3.6; canned products' -- wrong; there is no Annex I point 3.6 in this Regulation at all (metal sections run 3.1 Lead, 3.2 Cadmium, 3.3 Mercury, 3.4 Arsenic, 3.5 Tin, then jump straight to '4 Halogenated persistent organic pollutants' -- confirmed by direct section-header scan). Real pinpoint is 3.5.3.

discrepancies.food_category: Canned processed cereal-based foods and baby foods for infants and young children
discrepancies.evidence: 3.5.4 'Canned baby food and canned processed cereal-based food for infants and young children' = 50. Remark: 'Except canned dried and canned powdered products.'
discrepancies.note: Value/unit correct; same canned-dried/powdered exclusion applies as above, not captured in the JSON category label. JSON cites 'Section 3.6' (wrong); real section is 3.5.4; no 3.6 exists in this Regulation.

discrepancies.evidence: Real Cd (cow's-milk-based, powder): 'Cadmium | Säuglingsanfangsnahrung und Folgenahrung, die aus Kuhmilchproteinen oder Proteinhydrolysaten hergestellt wird | 0,01 | in Pulverform'. The JSON's 0,25 value instead matches 'Nickel | Säuglingsanfangsnahrung, Folgenahrung und Lebensmittel fur besondere medizinische Zwecke fur Sauglinge und Kleinkinder | 0,25 | in Pulverform' -- a DIFFERENT METAL's row in the same Annex 3 table.
discrepancies.note: CRITICAL: metal-identity swap. 0.25 mg/kg is the Swiss NICKEL infant-formula powder limit, not Cadmium's. Real Swiss Cd powder limits are 0.010 mg/kg (cow's-milk-based) / 0.020 mg/kg (soy-based) -- both roughly 12-25x lower than the JSON's stated 0.25. Cadmium is a Tier-1 zero-tolerance analyte under the HMTc framework; if 0.25 mg/kg were ever used as 'the Swiss regulatory ceiling' in a min(occurrence, government-ML) calculation, it would make the cap essentially never bind, silently erasing the intended ratchet. The JSON's own note field ('cadmium in soy-based formula 0.4 mg/kg') confirms the same swap -- 0.4 mg/kg is the Nickel soy-based-powder sub-value (same Annex 3 Nickel row), not Cadmium's real soy value of 0.02 mg/kg.

discrepancies.evidence: Real Cd (cow's-milk-based, liquid): 0,005 'flussig'. JSON's 0,1 matches Nickel's liquid infant-formula value ('... | 0,1 | flussig', same Nickel row).
discrepancies.note: Same metal-identity swap as the powder row. 0.1 mg/kg is Nickel's, not Cadmium's. Real Swiss Cd liquid limits are 0.005 mg/kg (cow's-milk-based) / 0.010 mg/kg (soy-based) -- 10-20x lower than stated.

discrepancies.food_category: Canned complementary foods for infants and young children
discrepancies.evidence: GB 2762-2022 Table 1 (both MAST and MAPAMA translations) has no canned-specific lead split; only the single 'Complementary foods for infants and young children ... 0.2' row exists. The value 0.25 appears instead in the SUPERSEDED GB 2762-2017 standard: 'Canned supplementary foods for infant and babies (excluding the products made from aquatic products and animal liver) ... 0.25' (China_GB2762-2017_FSIS_reference.txt, line 239-242).
discrepancies.note: HIGH-PRIORITY FINDING: this row cites instrument 'GB 2762-2022' but the 0.25 value is the OLD, superseded 2017 standard's canned-infant-food lead limit. GB 2762-2022 does not carry a canned-specific split for lead at all; the current applicable value for canned complementary foods would be the general 0.2 mg/kg complementary-food limit. This is a stale-standard citation error, not a translation artifact.

discrepancies.evidence: GB 2762-2022 Table 2 (Cadmium), 'food for special dietary use' section, contains exactly ONE infant-related row: 'Cereal Complementary Foods for Infants and Toddlers ... 0.06' (MAST) / 'Cereal-based complementary foods for infants and young children ... 0.06' (MAPAMA). No infant-formula cadmium row exists anywhere in Table 2, in either English translation.
discrepancies.note: GB 2762-2022 sets NO cadmium ML for infant formula (this is a real regulatory feature, confirmed independently in two English translations, and cadmium is likewise absent from the infant-formula section of the superseded 2017 standard). The value 0.01 exactly matches Codex CXS 193's Cd limit for 'Infant formula (ready to use)' (0.01 mg/kg) elsewhere in this same JSON file — strongly suggesting cross-jurisdiction value contamination (Codex value copied into the China row) rather than an actual China ML.

discrepancies.evidence: Same as above — Table 2 has no infant/follow-on/toddler formula cadmium row at all.
discrepancies.note: Same fabrication pattern as the 0-6mo Cd row; likely the same Codex 0.01 mg/kg value duplicated across both formula-stage rows.

discrepancies.food_category: Cereal-based complementary foods for infants and young children
discrepancies.evidence: MAST Table 2: 'Cereal Complementary Foods for Infants and Toddlers ... 0.06'. MAPAMA Table 2: 'Cereal-based complementary foods for infants and young children ... 0.06'. Confirmed identically in both independent English translations.
discrepancies.note: The JSON value 0.05 exactly matches Codex CXS 193's Cd limit for 'Processed cereal-based foods for infants and young children' (0.05 mg/kg, same JSON file, Codex section) — another likely instance of the Codex value bleeding into the China row instead of China's actual (stricter) 0.06 mg/kg.

discrepancies.evidence: GB 2762-2022 Table 3 (Mercury), 'food for special dietary use' section, contains exactly ONE infant-related row: 'Canned Complementary Foods for Infants and Toddlers ... 0.02' (total mercury). No infant-formula mercury row exists in Table 3 in either translation.
discrepancies.note: GB 2762-2022 sets no mercury ML for infant formula at all.

discrepancies.food_category: Cereal-based complementary foods for infants and young children
discrepancies.evidence: MAST Table 3: 'food for special dietary use ... Canned Complementary Foods for Infants and Toddlers 0.02' (total mercury). MAPAMA Table 3: 'Canned Complementary Foods for Infants and Young Children 0.02'.
discrepancies.note: Numeric value (0.02) is correct but the food_category is WRONG: the primary source's only infant-related mercury row is for CANNED complementary foods, not cereal-based. GB 2762-2022 sets no mercury limit for cereal-based complementary foods at all — the category label was swapped with 'canned'.

discrepancies.evidence: GB 2762-2022 Table 4 (Arsenic), 'food for special dietary use' section, lists only complementary-food rows (cereal-based excl./incl. algae, canned excl./incl. aquatic-or-liver, food supplements, sports nutrition food, pregnancy/lactation supplements). No 'infant formula' row of any kind — rice-based or otherwise — appears in Table 4 in either English translation.
discrepancies.note: No infant-formula arsenic limit exists in GB 2762-2022 Table 4. Notably, this exact value (0.1 mg/kg, rice-based infant formula, inorganic arsenic) also appears verbatim in this JSON's South Korea rows for the same food category — suggesting cross-jurisdiction contamination (Korea value copied into China, or a shared template value applied to both).

discrepancies.evidence: Same as above — Table 4 has no infant-formula row, rice-based or non-rice.
discrepancies.note: Same fabrication pattern. This exact value (0.02) also appears in this JSON's South Korea 'Infant formula (non-rice, powder)' row, which is itself unsupported by the Korea source — same value propagated across two jurisdictions with no primary-text anchor in either.

discrepancies.evidence: MAPAMA Table 4: 'Cereal-Based Complementary foods for infants and young children (excluding products that add algae) ... Total arsenic: — / Inorganic Arsenic: 0.2'. The total-arsenic column is explicitly dashed out ('—' = no limit set); only inorganic arsenic is limited.
discrepancies.note: WRONG SPECIATION — exactly the iAs/tAs distinction this audit was asked to watch for. The 0.2 mg/kg value in the primary text is an INORGANIC arsenic limit; GB 2762-2022 sets no total-arsenic limit for this category at all. The JSON's 'Arsenic (total)' / 'total arsenic' labeling is incorrect. Also, the primary source's actual split is 'excluding algae-added products' vs. 'algae-added products' (0.2 vs 0.3), not 'rice' vs. 'non-rice' as the food_category implies.

discrepancies.evidence: Same underlying primary row as above: 'Cereal-Based Complementary foods for infants and young children (excluding products that add algae) ... Inorganic Arsenic: 0.2'.
discrepancies.note: Metal and speciation label (iAs) are correct here and the value matches, but the food_category framing is fabricated: GB 2762-2022's Table 4 has no 'rice-based vs. non-rice' split for infant complementary foods. The real split governing this 0.2 value is algae-added vs. non-algae-added. This row and the 'Arsenic (total) / non-rice' row above appear to be two different, both-inaccurate redescriptions of the same single primary-source line.

discrepancies.evidence: FSS (Contaminants) Regulations 2011, Regulation 2.1.1, Table, item 1 Lead: '(ic) Infant Milk substitute and Infant foods ... 0.2' (parts per million by weight).
discrepancies.note: JSON value is exactly 10x too low (0.02 vs. actual 0.2 mg/kg). The value 0.02 exactly matches Codex CXS 193's Pb limit for 'Infant formula (ready to use)' (0.02 mg/kg, liquid/ready-to-use basis) elsewhere in this JSON — likely cross-jurisdiction/basis contamination (Codex ready-to-use value substituted for India's powder-basis value).

discrepancies.evidence: FSS (Contaminants) Regulations 2011, Table, item 6 Cadmium: '(i) Infant Milk substitute and Infant foods ... 0.1'.
discrepancies.note: JSON value is exactly 10x too low (0.01 vs. actual 0.1 mg/kg). 0.01 exactly matches Codex CXS 193's Cd limit for 'Infant formula (ready to use)' — same cross-jurisdiction contamination pattern seen in the India Pb row and the China Cd rows above.

discrepancies.evidence: Same primary row: '(i) Infant Milk substitute and Infant foods ... 0.1' (no separate cereal-based split exists in India's regulation).
discrepancies.note: JSON value (0.05) matches Codex's Cd cereal-based complementary food value, not India's actual combined 0.1 mg/kg limit. This is the fourth instance in this audit of a Codex value appearing to substitute for the correct country-specific value.

discrepancies.evidence: FSS (Contaminants) Regulations 2011, Table, item 3 Arsenic: 'Infant Milk substitute and Infant foods ... 0.05'.
discrepancies.note: JSON value is 2x too high (0.1 vs. actual 0.05 mg/kg). Primary text labels this simply 'Arsenic' with no explicit total/inorganic qualifier (a 2011 regulation predating iAs-specific speciation practice); treating it as total arsenic per JSON's speciation label is a reasonable but not textually-certain interpretation.

discrepancies.evidence: Same primary row: 'Infant Milk substitute and Infant foods ... 0.05' (no separate cereal-based split exists in the regulation).
discrepancies.note: Same 2x-too-high error as the infant-formula As row above; both JSON rows draw on the same single combined 0.05 mg/kg primary value.

discrepancies.evidence: FSS (Contaminants) Regulations 2011, Table, item 7 Mercury: 'Fish ... 0.5 / Other foods ... 1.0'; item 8 Methyl Mercury: 'All foods ... 0.25'. No infant-specific mercury row exists anywhere in the regulation.
discrepancies.note: India's 2011 Contaminants Regulations set no infant-specific mercury ML. The generic 'Other foods' (1.0) or 'Methyl Mercury — All foods' (0.25) categories would be the only applicable defaults; 0.01 does not correspond to any value in the primary text.

discrepancies.evidence: FSS (Contaminants) Regulations 2011, Table, item 4 Tin: '(i) Processed and canned products ... 250.0' (general) vs. '(i-b) Infant Milk substitute and Infant foods ... 5.0' (infant-specific).
discrepancies.note: MOST SIGNIFICANT FINDING IN THIS AUDIT: India's law carries a dedicated, much stricter infant-specific tin limit (5.0 mg/kg) that is 50x lower than the general canned/processed-food limit (250 mg/kg) the JSON used. The JSON's note field ('General canned food limit applies; no infant-specific Sn limit') is factually incorrect — an infant-specific limit does exist and directly governs this food category. Using 250 mg/kg as India's infant-food tin ceiling would misstate the legal limit by 50x in the permissive direction.

discrepancies.evidence: Korea_USDA_GAIN_FAIRS_2022, p.23, 'Heavy Metal Standards for Processed Food Products' table: 'Infant formula, follow-up formula, cereal based formula for infant/young children, other food for infant/young children, special formula for infant/young children, follow-up milk formula' — Lead (mg/kg): 'Not more than 0.01'. Confirmed by direct visual inspection of the PDF page image (table cell alignment is ambiguous in plain pdftotext extraction).
discrepancies.note: SECONDARY SOURCE: this is a USDA FAS GAIN report summarizing Korea's MFDS Food Code, not the sovereign Korean text — treat with corresponding caution. JSON value (0.02) is 2x the value this summary reports (0.01).

discrepancies.food_category: Processed cereal-based foods for infants and young children
discrepancies.evidence: Same table/row as above — the single combined target-food row ('...cereal based formula for infant/young children...') covers cereal-based formula at Lead 'Not more than 0.01'; there is no separate cereal-based Pb value in this source.
discrepancies.note: SECONDARY SOURCE (USDA GAIN summary). JSON value (0.2) is 20x the value this summary reports (0.01) and exactly matches Codex CXS 193's Pb limit for 'Processed cereal-based foods for infants and young children' (0.2 mg/kg) — again consistent with the Codex-value-substitution pattern seen repeatedly in this audit.

discrepancies.evidence: The word 'Cadmium' appears in this document only in the 'Heavy Metals in Agricultural Products', 'Heavy Metals in Livestock Products', and 'Heavy Metals in Fishery Products' tables (raw commodities — grains, meat, fish). The infant-formula-specific 'Heavy Metal Standards for Processed Food Products' table has only Lead, Arsenic, and Inorganic Arsenic columns — no Cadmium column at all.
discrepancies.note: SECONDARY SOURCE (USDA GAIN summary): this report contains no cadmium data for infant/processed foods whatsoever. 0.01 may be a real MFDS Food Code value, but it cannot be verified from this cited source_doc.

discrepancies.food_category: Processed cereal-based foods for infants and young children
discrepancies.evidence: Same as above — no Cadmium column exists in the processed/infant food heavy-metal table in this document.
discrepancies.note: SECONDARY SOURCE. Not verifiable from Korea_USDA_GAIN_FAIRS_2022.pdf. Value (0.05) also matches the recurring Codex cereal-Cd figure seen elsewhere in this audit.

discrepancies.evidence: 'Mercury' appears in this document only in the 'Heavy Metals in Fishery Products' table (fish/mollusks/crustaceans/seaweed). No Mercury column exists in the 'Heavy Metal Standards for Processed Food Products' table that covers infant formula.
discrepancies.note: SECONDARY SOURCE: this report contains no mercury data for infant/processed foods. Not verifiable from the cited source_doc.

discrepancies.evidence: Same table/row: the 'Arsenic (mg/kg)' [total] column is blank ('-') for the infant formula row, and the only Inorganic Arsenic value shown (0.1) is explicitly restricted to rice-derived-ingredient products. No separate non-rice value of any kind appears for this row.
discrepancies.note: SECONDARY SOURCE. No non-rice-specific iAs value is reported in this document for infant formula. 0.02 is identical to the equally-unsupported China 'non-rice infant formula' iAs value elsewhere in this JSON, suggesting a shared fabricated/templated figure rather than an independently sourced Korean value.

discrepancies.evidence: The word 'tin' (as the metal Sn) does not appear anywhere in this document.
discrepancies.note: SECONDARY SOURCE: this USDA GAIN report contains no tin/Sn data at all, for any food category. The JSON note ('General canned food limit applies') is not supported by anything in the cited source_doc — this report simply does not address tin.

discrepancies.food_category: Cereal-based foods for child nutrition (infants and young children)
discrepancies.evidence: ANEXO I, 1.3 Lead: "Cereal-based foods for child nutrition (infants and young children) | 0.05" (immediately below "Sugars | 0.10" and above "Transition foods for infants and young children | 0.15").
discrepancies.note: JSON value (0.1 mg/kg) is 2x the actual primary MTL (0.05 mg/kg). Also wrong table citation ("Table 1.2", should be 1.3). This is a genuine numeric error, not a rounding or unit issue -- the correct Brazilian lead MTL for baby cereal is half of what the JSON states.

discrepancies.food_category: Transition foods for infants and young children
discrepancies.evidence: ANEXO I, 1.3 Lead: "Transition foods for infants and young children | 0.15" (directly below the Cereal-based-foods row, 0.05).
discrepancies.note: JSON understates the primary MTL (0.1 vs actual 0.15 mg/kg). Combined with the previous row, both Brazil Lead "cereal-based" and "transition foods" JSON values look transposed/averaged from the real 0.05 and 0.15 figures, landing on 0.1 for both -- possibly cross-contaminated with Cadmium's real "Transition foods" value of 0.10 mg/kg (see next row).

discrepancies.evidence: ANEXO I, 1.6 Total mercury contains exactly five rows: Crustaceans (0.50), Bivalve mollusks (0.50), Cephalopod mollusks (0.50), Predator fish (1.00), Fish except predators (0.50). The word "mercury" occurs nowhere else in the 1,427-line primary-text extraction. There is no infant-formula or child-nutrition row anywhere in the mercury table.
discrepancies.note: Fabrication / cross-contamination, not a citation slip. Brazil's ANVISA IN 88/2021 does not regulate mercury in infant formula or baby food at all -- its mercury MTLs cover only seafood. The JSON's value (0.005 mg/kg) exactly equals Codex's real Hg-infant-formula ML found elsewhere in this same JSON file, suggesting the Codex figure was copy-pasted onto the Brazil row. The JSON notes also cite "Table 1.4," which is actually Copper's section, not Mercury's (real Mercury section is 1.6). This is the most serious defect found in the Brazil dataset.

discrepancies.evidence: Same 1.6 Total mercury table as above -- no cereal-based / child-nutrition entry exists; only the five seafood categories are regulated for mercury in this document.
discrepancies.note: Fabrication / cross-contamination. The JSON's value (0.01 mg/kg) exactly equals the EU's real Hg ML for "Infant formulae and follow-on formulae" (Reg. 2023/915, Annex I 3.3) found elsewhere in this same JSON file, suggesting the EU figure was copy-pasted onto the Brazil "cereal-based foods" row under the wrong metal/category combination entirely. Brazil ANVISA IN 88/2021 sets no mercury limit for any infant/child food category.

discrepancies.evidence: Guidance Sec. I, footnote 2: "This guidance does not apply to infant formula or any beverages, including toddler drinks." Sec. III.B, footnote 13: "Infant formula and bottled water labeled for infants are also collected through the TDS program but were not included in this analysis. TDS infant formula data ... indicate that the majority of samples collected contain no measurable concentration of lead (<limit of detection, which is 4.0 ppb)."
discrepancies.note: Correctly absent from JSON -- FDA's lead action-level guidance explicitly excludes infant formula and all beverages from its scope. No FDA lead ML/action level exists for infant formula; this is confirmed, not a gap. Listed here for completeness since the task asked to watch for this exclusion.

discrepancies.food_category: Processed cereal-based foods for infants and young children
discrepancies.evidence: Codex_CXS193_2023.pdf LEAD table runs from "Assorted (sub)tropical fruits" through "Wine | 0.2" (~90 rows); no row for cereal-based foods for infants/young children exists. Confirmed also absent from the LEAD section of the sibling Codex_CXS193_2015.pdf.
discrepancies.note: Not found in either Codex source file available in this source package. Cannot verify; likely sourced from general knowledge of a later CCCF amendment not captured in either local PDF.

discrepancies.food_category: Canned baby foods / other foods for infants and young children
discrepancies.evidence: No "baby food" or "canned infant/baby" row exists anywhere in Codex_CXS193_2023.pdf (zero hits for "baby food" in the full-text extraction). Confirmed also absent from Codex_CXS193_2015.pdf.
discrepancies.note: Not found in either Codex source file in the package.

discrepancies.evidence: Codex_CXS193_2023.pdf CADMIUM table lists only: Brassica/bulb/fruiting/leafy/legume vegetables, potato, pulses, root/tuber and stalk/stem vegetables, cereal grains, rice polished (0.4), wheat, marine bivalve molluscs, cephalopods, natural mineral waters, salt -- no infant formula row. Confirmed also absent from the CADMIUM table of Codex_CXS193_2015.pdf (same row set, same absence).
discrepancies.note: Not found in either Codex source file. Codex has no Cadmium ML for infant formula in either vintage captured in this repo.

discrepancies.food_category: Processed cereal-based foods for infants and young children
discrepancies.evidence: Same CADMIUM table as above -- no cereal-based-foods-for-infants row in either Codex file.
discrepancies.note: Not found in either Codex source file.

discrepancies.evidence: Codex_CXS193_2023.pdf ARSENIC table lists only: edible fats/oils, margarine, minarine, named animal fats, olive oil (refined/virgin), olive residue oil, vegetable oils (crude/edible), natural mineral waters, salt. No rice entry and no numeric inorganic-arsenic ML anywhere in this file's Arsenic section (only a PTWI reference to inorganic arsenic in the toxicological-guidance text, no ML row).
discrepancies.note: Not found in Codex_CXS193_2023.pdf. HOWEVER: this exact value IS present in the sibling file Codex_CXS193_2015.pdf, ARSENIC table: "Rice, polished | 0.2 | Whole commodity | ... The ML is for inorganic arsenic (As-in). Countries or importers may decide to use their own screening ...". So the JSON's number is real Codex content (adopted ML for iAs in polished rice), just not verifiable from the specific file the JSON cites as its source. The citation should point to a document that actually contains this ML.

discrepancies.evidence: ARSENIC table (see above) has no infant-formula row in either Codex_CXS193_2023.pdf or Codex_CXS193_2015.pdf.
discrepancies.note: Not found in either Codex source file in the package.

discrepancies.food_category: Processed cereal-based foods for infants and young children
discrepancies.evidence: Not present in the ARSENIC table of either Codex file. Note: Codex_CXS193_2015.pdf does have a "Cereal-based foods for infants and young children | 200 µg/kg" row, but it is under DEOXYNIVALENOL (a mycotoxin ML), not Arsenic -- unrelated to this JSON row despite the similar category name.
discrepancies.note: Not found under Arsenic in either Codex file. The superficially similar 200 µg/kg cereal-based-foods figure that does exist in the 2015 file is for a different contaminant (DON) entirely and must not be confused with an arsenic value.

discrepancies.evidence: Codex_CXS193_2023.pdf MERCURY table contains exactly two rows: Natural mineral waters (0.001 mg/l) and Salt, food grade (0.1). METHYLMERCURY table contains exactly two rows: Fish (0.5 GL, except predatory) and Predatory fish (1 GL). No infant-formula row under either heading, in either Codex file.
discrepancies.note: Not found in either Codex source file. Separately, the JSON row itself is internally inconsistent: metal field says "Mercury (Hg)" and speciation says "total", but the notes field says "methylmercury" -- total mercury and methylmercury are a non-negotiable distinction (tHg vs MeHg) and should never be used interchangeably in the same row. This is a data-quality defect independent of whether the source is found.

discrepancies.food_category: Canned infant formula and baby foods
discrepancies.evidence: Codex_CXS193_2023.pdf TIN table: "Canned foods (other than beverages) | 250 | C | ML"; "Canned beverages | 150 | C | ML"; plus ~20 specific canned-commodity rows (fruits, vegetables, cured meats) at 250 or 50 mg/kg depending on container type. No infant-formula- or baby-food-specific row exists. Same result in Codex_CXS193_2015.pdf TIN table.
discrepancies.note: Not found in either Codex source file. The 50 mg/kg figure is plausible on its face -- it exactly matches Brazil's own "Canned child foods" inorganic-tin MTL (verified above) and the EU's "Canned infant formulae and follow-on formulae" Sn ML (50 mg/kg, Reg. 2023/915 Annex I 3.6, present elsewhere in this same JSON file) -- but it is not verifiable from either Codex primary source in this package. General Codex canned-food Sn ceiling in the verified text is 250 mg/kg, not infant-specific.
